summary:
GazeCheck is a 1-minute eye-movement self-test that helps spot fatigue and neuro-ocular changes in astronauts during long-duration missions.

We built GazeCheck, a Python app that turns an ordinary laptop webcam into an eye-movement health check. It uses MediaPipe to track the irises while the astronaut does three short tasks: a quick calibration, following a gliding dot (smooth pursuit) and looking at a dot that jumps left or right (saccades). The app measures reaction time, tracking lag and tracking quality. It compares them with the astronaut’s own baseline and shows a green, yellow or red status with a clear action, from “no action needed” to “report to the flight surgeon.”

On long missions, astronauts must notice changes in their own health. Eye movements are a sensitive, non-invasive signal of fatigue, sleep loss and changes to the vestibular and visual systems. These include Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), which NASA’s Human Research Program studies. GazeCheck needs no extra hardware, takes about a minute and gives astronauts an objective daily measure they can act on themselves. It’s a prototype: its alert thresholds are illustrative and still need clinical validation.
details:
The app is tracking eye movements which are are a sensitive, non-invasive signal into how fatigue an individual is based on a given baseline recorded when individual is well rested and in optimal conditions (i.e. before spaceflight)

It takes only a minute to take this test which is always compared to the individual's baseline.

The app requires a webcam and a well lit face so the eyes can be tracked.
